content: Liberia developed its first National Priority Assistive Products List (APL) in 2021 as part of a broader national strategy to improve access to assistive technology. This initiative was led by the Ministries of Health and Gender, Children, and Social Protection, in collaboration with the National Commission on Disabilities and organizations representing people with disabilities. The process began with an assessment of the country’s assistive technology capacity, followed by stakeholder workshops to create and validate the APL. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) Priority Assistive Products List was reviewed and adapted to Liberia’s specific needs, priorities, and resources. The final APL included two types of manual wheelchairs among 33 other assistive products. The APL serves as a foundation for further national actions, such as developing technical standards for regulating assistive technology imports, creating quality checklists and service delivery guidelines, advocating for funding and prioritization of assistive products, training service providers, improving data coverage, and integrating assistive technology into other national policies. Priority product lists should include detailed product specifications to aid procurement and criteria for selecting the most appropriate wheelchair in collaboration with users. The quality and durability of wheelchairs can be assessed using international or national product standards. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has established standards for wheelchairs (ISO 7176 series), wheelchair cushions (ISO 16840 Part 2), and postural support devices (ISO 16840 Part 3). These standards address safety and performance for a broad population. Some regions and countries, such as Europe, Australia, and New Zealand, have developed additional standards tailored to their contexts, such as EN 12183 and AS/NZS 3695-1 for manual wheelchairs. These standards build on ISO testing and results. Wheelchair provision guidelines emphasize that not all users’ needs can be met with pre-selected products, so flexibility to explore alternative options is essential. Regular market evaluations ensure the most suitable products are available. Proper wheelchair fitting is critical to prevent harm and ensure user satisfaction. The WHO’s wheelchair service provision steps, including individual fitting, are feasible across income settings and benefit all users. The preparation and fitting process involves assembling the wheelchair, adjusting components, and ensuring it meets the user’s needs for mobility, posture, and function. This process may require multiple appointments and adjustments to achieve optimal fit. Training is essential for wheelchair users and their assistants to maximize the wheelchair’s benefits and avoid harm. Training should cover skills for using the wheelchair, operating its components, guiding others, and performing maintenance and repairs. The training can be delivered in person or online and may occur over one or several days. Even experienced users benefit from task-specific training, especially when transitioning to a new wheelchair, experiencing changes in health or environment, or entering different life stages. For example, as a child becomes more independent or an older adult’s needs evolve, training requirements may change. Task-specific training includes skills such as transferring in and out of the wheelchair, repositioning, relieving pressure, and navigating various environments. Users should also learn to guide others assisting them and operate wheelchair components like locks, cushions, and footrests. Maintenance training includes cleaning, lubricating, and repairing parts like cushions, tires, and batteries. Assistance from others, such as family, caregivers, or the public, may be needed in different settings, and users should be empowered to instruct others on how to assist safely and effectively. Proper training and fitting are crucial to preventing product abandonment and secondary injuries. Wheelchair services should allocate sufficient time for fitting and training, and users may need follow-up adjustments after using the wheelchair in their daily environments.
